title: ATLAS: Constraints-Aware Multi-Agent Collaboration for Real-World Travel Planning
one_liner: Use multiple planning agents that track constraints, critique drafts, and keep searching until the trip plan satisfies the real travel rules.
lead: Travel planning looks simple until the real constraints pile up. A user may need specific dates, prices, locations, transfer limits, and changing preferences, while the available flights and hotels can also change during the interaction. Single-agent planners often fail because they miss constraints or stop searching too early. This paper proposes ATLAS, a multi-agent framework for travel planning that separates the work into constraint management, plan critique, and adaptive search. The central claim is that travel plans improve when constraints are tracked explicitly and when several specialized agents repeatedly inspect and revise the plan, because missed constraints and weak search results are caught before the final itinerary is returned.

problem.h2: Why travel planning breaks under real constraints
paras: A valid trip plan must satisfy many rules at once: budget, timing, locations, user preferences, and availability in the external world. Some rules are written directly by the user, while others are implied by the situation, such as the time needed between connections.

The planning problem is hard because these constraints interact. A hotel choice can force a different arrival airport. A cheaper flight can create an impossible transfer because its arrival time may leave too little time for the next leg. A user correction in the middle of the conversation can invalidate the whole draft. The planner therefore needs to keep a live picture of which constraints are active and whether the current itinerary still satisfies them.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Assign separate agents to track constraints, critique drafts, and search for better options so that the final itinerary is revised until it satisfies the active travel rules.

panels.title: 1. User states a trip goal
panels.caption: The request includes explicit and implicit travel rules.

panels.title: 2. Constraint agent records rules
panels.caption: A dedicated component keeps track of what the itinerary must satisfy.

panels.title: 3. Planner drafts an itinerary
panels.caption: Another agent searches the world and assembles candidate travel options.

panels.title: 4. Critic checks the draft
panels.viz_args: which rules are broken or underspecified?
panels.caption: A critique step finds missing constraints and weak choices.

panels.title: 5. Revise and search again
panels.caption: The loop continues until the itinerary satisfies the constraint set.

steps.text: A constraint manager gathers rules from the user request, the conversation history, and the current world state.
Planning agents query tools or sources to find flights, stays, and route choices that could satisfy those rules.
The system combines candidate options into a complete trip proposal.
A critique agent checks for broken rules, missing information, and low-quality decisions.
The search and critique loop repeats until the itinerary passes the active rule checks because unresolved violations trigger another search round.

paras: The paper changes travel planning from one long monologue into a coordinated system of roles. The key object is a constraint-tracked itinerary that is repeatedly checked and revised as external information and user feedback change.
object.object: a constraint-tracked itinerary revised by multiple specialized agents

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: constraint satisfaction state
hidden.name: which travel rules are currently satisfied, violated, or still unknown
paras: The planner only succeeds if it knows the state of each relevant constraint. A draft itinerary can look plausible while still breaking a budget cap, missing a visa timing rule, or relying on an impossible connection.

The paper's real target is therefore a live constraint satisfaction state. That state must be updated whenever the plan changes or new world information arrives. Without it, the system cannot tell whether a revision helped or simply moved the failure from one part of the trip to another.

heat.caption: The planner needs a live map of rule status so that each revision can be judged against the same travel constraints.

reads.html: A travel plan is only good when the system knows which rules it already satisfies and which rules it still breaks.
ATLAS tracks explicit, implicit, and changing constraints throughout the planning loop, then uses critique and search updates to drive the itinerary toward full satisfaction.

mechanism.h2: Why multiple specialized agents can help
paras: Travel planning mixes different kinds of work: remembering rules, exploring options, and checking whether the current draft is still valid. One agent can do all of that in principle, but errors accumulate because those tasks compete for limited planning focus.

A multi-agent system can help by assigning those responsibilities explicitly. Constraint tracking prevents the rules from getting lost. Critique exposes hidden failures before the trip is returned. Adaptive search reopens the world lookup when the current draft does not work. The gain comes from repeated correction, because each specialized role can catch errors the others leave behind.

stages.s: user goal plus live travel data

math.h2: A compact statement of the planner target
math.words: Prefer itineraries that satisfy more constraints and pay less travel cost, while penalizing every unresolved violation.
math.equation: plan_score(itinerary) = travel_value(itinerary) - alpha * violation_count(itinerary) - beta * unknown_constraint_count(itinerary)
symbols: the overall usefulness of the itinerary, including cost, timing, and fit to user preferences
how many active travel rules the itinerary currently breaks
how many relevant rules still have unresolved status
the penalty weight for each known rule violation
the penalty weight for each still-unchecked rule
the value used to compare candidate itineraries

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose itinerary A has travel_value = 80, but it breaks one timing rule and leaves one hotel rule unchecked.
Itinerary B has travel_value = 74 and no known violations or unknown rules.
Even though A looked better at first, B wins because it satisfies the full rule set more reliably.
This is why critique and re-search matter: they expose hidden failures before the planner commits to a glossy but invalid trip.

math.note: Penalizing unresolved rules is important because a travel plan is not trustworthy when some key constraints have never been checked.

charts.title: Single-agent travel planning
charts.note: A single planner can search and draft, but it often loses track of interacting rules because all planning responsibilities stay inside one loop.

charts.title: ATLAS
charts.note: The multi-agent design improves final itineraries by making rule tracking and critique first-class parts of the planning process.

items.html: If an implicit travel requirement is never recorded, the rest of the system cannot protect it, so the final itinerary may fail in practice even when internal checks look clean.
Flights and rooms change quickly, so a plan can become invalid after it was drafted unless the search stage refreshes critical facts before final return.

items.b: The critic finds problems but the planner cannot repair them.
items.html: A critique-only loop is not enough. The search stage must be able to reopen the world lookup and explore better options when a violation is found, because the current candidate set may contain no valid repair.
The framework works when constraints are tracked explicitly, critique is strong enough to surface hidden failures, and the planner keeps searching until every important rule has a verified status.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a travel-planning interface with live or recorded flight and hotel data, then ask it to satisfy multi-stop itineraries under budget and timing rules. Show the active constraint list, the current itinerary, the critic's violation report, and the next revision after each planning round. Compare a single-agent planner against ATLAS on whether the returned trip satisfies all constraints after user follow-up questions.
demo.metric_eq: final_pass_rate = valid_returned_itineraries / total_requests; missed_rule_rate = overlooked_constraints / total_constraints
demo.closing: The useful result is an itinerary that survives real constraint checks, not just an itinerary that sounds plausible.
